section.title: Getting to Staff: Scope, Promotion Timing, and Visibility at Big Tech
section.deck: Five panelists on reaching staff argue that high-scope work, early and explicit promotion conversations, willingness to take feedback, and visibility matter more than title alone.

blocks.text: Editorial summary of the panel's shared view: the opening framing treats staff as the first level where an individual contributor must lead without managing people. Progression runs from tasks to features to projects, and then to several projects or a whole product. The panelists argue that reaching that level depends on choosing work with real scope and visible impact, asking for promotion early and explicitly, and then acting on feedback. They also say title opens doors without settling scope, that managers differ in how much they control promotion, and that infrastructure and product teams offer different routes. Several points are offered as personal experience rather than general rules.
blocks.heading: The panel's view: scope, early asking, and visibility shape the path to staff

blocks.question: How do you tell which problems are worth solving, when a staff promotion needs enough scope?
answer: Zach describes a move at Netflix from an automated threat-detection project, which looked too ambitious, to a shared graph database that other teams could use in many cases. The shift brought more pay, more respect, and a larger leadership role.

Zach adds that scope is not the only test. Risky projects that may never pan out also waste time. Senior engineers can judge how much impact a project will have before investing in it, so a small request to them may sit in a backlog.

followups.question: How do you build the judgment to see which work will matter?
answer: Ryan says the main method is to read the incentives of the organization. Most teams publish plans with metric targets, so a person can compare an idea with a team goal and judge whether it is large enough.
Ryan also worked on an ads project outside Ryan's own team, which no one assigned, because the revenue opportunity looked large. The work had clear impact and was linked to a senior promotion.

blocks.question: For Carly and Lee: how explicit should someone be about wanting to reach staff, and how much should they tell a manager?
answer: Carly manages staff engineers and says people raise promotion in different ways. In Carly's experience, about half of the requests to move to staff came from people who were not yet ready. The other half came from people who were ready long before they asked. Carly sees two groups: people who ask readily, sometimes before they are ready, and people who wait until readiness is proved, often a year past it.
Carly suggests reflecting honestly on readiness without setting the bar so high that a reserved person holds back.

Lee says promotions often trail performance at large tech companies, so a person who never raises the question may not know what is missing. Lee suggests stating the goal directly: a wish to grow on the technical track rather than into management. Ask what is missing, build a plan, and write down the evidence, so the manager has the material when the person is ready. Lee notes that not everyone wants a promotion, and some people prefer their current level.

followups.question: Should a manager wait to be asked, or raise a promotion first?
answer: Carly says both happen. Carly has raised promotions with people who did not ask, when Carly judged them ready. With a large team, year-end reviews are the main time to reflect, but Carly prefers that people speak up between reviews when they feel ready or are clearly above the bar. Carly calls waiting a passive approach and sees little downside to asking too early.

followups.question: What should someone do if their manager says they are not ready?
answer: Carly says to listen. Feedback usually points to a blind spot the person cannot see, and a well-meaning manager is not trying to block a ready person. Carly also treats the response to feedback as part of readiness. A staff engineer must take feedback from leaders and teams, act on it, and reflect on it without turning combative.

Another panelist describes a first attempt to promote them into a manager role at Amazon that did not go through. The panelist asked which objections were raised and what evidence would answer each one, then tracked those gaps. The promotion came later, and the panelist says the change was the response to feedback, not one more project.

followups.question: What if you disagree with the feedback?
answer: A panelist says that if you disagree and think the feedback is wrong, you can test it by interviewing elsewhere, because the market gives its own view of readiness. The panelist has been promoted internally only once, from junior to mid-level, and got later promotions by changing companies. Some feedback is unreasonable, the panelist says, but learning to take feedback still matters, and leaving is one valid option rather than a required one.

followups.question: How should someone phrase a request for promotion?
answer: A panelist says framing matters. A new hire who asks for a promotion right away is unlikely to get support. A better frame is to name a first goal, such as ramping up and having impact, and ask for a check-in in about three months to plan the path. A manager is likely to agree, because the request then shows both interest in promotion and sound priorities.

Another panelist says asking early and explicitly is worth doing, even when it feels uncomfortable. At each level, that panelist asked what it would take to reach the next one, and the manager was glad to help because the team gained impact. Once a promotion looked likely, the panelist also asked about the level after that.

blocks.question: Does a high performer have leverage with a manager?
answer: A panelist says strong performers have leverage inside a company, because a manager wants to keep someone who solves the team's problems. Asking for growth from that position is more likely to get a receptive response than asking from a less central role.

The same panelist names the limits. A manager cannot promote someone on request, because processes and other decision-makers are involved. A manager can still steer projects toward the gaps named in a promotion plan. If the current team cannot offer that work, the honest options are to move to another team or look outside.

blocks.question: How much control does a manager have over promotion at each level?
answer: Zach says that at Airbnb, managers decided promotions up to senior, while promotion from senior to staff and above went through a committee. Zach describes Amazon before it used committees for promotion, where decisions moved up the management chain through skip-level managers and directors above the senior level, not only the direct manager.

followups.question: How does the process change at the highest levels?
answer: A panelist says that from junior to mid-level, the direct manager's view is usually decisive, so alignment with the manager matters most there. At the highest levels, sign-off from VPs and other senior leaders is needed, and the manager becomes more of a messenger for the committee. That is why it helps to ask early, so the manager can collect the committee's feedback sooner.

blocks.question: How should someone judge which team is the best place to earn a staff promotion?
answer: A panelist offers a rough test. At a company with many products, a team that works on the core product usually has more visibility than a team on a side product. The panelist jokes that working on a smaller app such as Garage Band is unlikely to lead to a promotion, while the flagship product gives visibility almost for free.

Another panelist says a team with less visibility can still make progress. Find the team that owns a weak spot, show them the problem in their code, and offer to help or pair with them. Fixing a real problem with that team makes a person a strong partner, which is different from a small cosmetic change.

A third panelist says caring about the work matters as much as its impact. During a Google interview, that panelist was offered an ads role and said it did not interest them. Work a person cares about gets their best effort, and that makes it easier to advocate for the product to others.

blocks.question: Do product or infrastructure teams offer a clearer route to staff?
answer: Ryan says staff-level opportunities are more common on infrastructure teams. Ryan's view is that product engineers usually reach high impact past senior by leading large projects, and there are few such seats. Infrastructure work has leverage built in, because foundational technology helps many teams move faster, which creates more roles. Ryan says Ryan's own infrastructure team is quite senior compared with others.

followups.question: Does the same leverage show up in data and engineering roles?
answer: Zach follows up with experience in both kinds of role. At Netflix, Zach was a staff-level tech lead on an infrastructure team building a graph database. At Airbnb, Zach was a tech lead on pricing and availability, which was closer to product. Zach says data engineering shows the difference most clearly. The more a person changes how other engineers do their work, rather than building one pipeline, the more leverage they have.

followups.question: Does infrastructure work lead to promotion on its own?
answer: A panelist agrees with Ryan's point and adds that changing how other engineers work, such as saving each engineer a few minutes a day, scales across hundreds of engineers. Then the panelist frames it differently. Infrastructure work often spans several teams and can have built-in impact, but the question is what impact is actually available, whether managers in that area know how to promote people, and who sees the work. If only the most senior person on a team sees it, the work may not support a promotion. Infrastructure teams offer more chances, but the team setup still matters, and product work is not ruled out.

blocks.question: How do remote or hybrid engineers compete with colleagues who sit close to the manager?
answer: A panelist says the main answer is documentation, communication, and proof. Written evidence of impact lets the manager and others see the work without relying on physical proximity. The panelist has worked only in fully remote settings, so the hybrid case is an extrapolation.

blocks.question: Did staff promotion require unusually long hours?
answer: Panelists give mixed accounts. One says the project that led to promotion took more than 40 hours a week. Zach recalls about 50 to 55 hours, including the Netflix graph-database build. Another panelist says 50 to 60 hours was common but still left time for sleep. A further panelist notes that some people are promoted while working 40 hours.

Panelists who moved into management say hours mattered less. One says that as a manager, the panelist did not exceed 40 hours a week, and that multiplying other people's output shows impact in fewer hours than personal delivery. Another plans by goal rather than hours, working around 60 hours one week and around 30 the next.

blocks.question: Do inflated startup titles lead to down-leveling at big tech?
answer: A panelist says down-leveling happens when a candidate does not meet the level the company expects. The panelist does not think it can be avoided, except by being stronger or interviewing better. Startup titles are often inflated, so the panelist advises comparing the scope of the work with what each company expects at each level, rather than targeting a title.

Another panelist says title matters less than pay and meaningful work. That panelist moved from a mid-level role at a startup to a junior role at Facebook, for about an 80 percent pay increase, and calls that a good trade.

blocks.question: Seniority opens doors, but bigger projects tend to come after promotion. How do you break that cycle?
answer: A panelist says seniority helps but matters less than internal brand. The person a manager or director thinks of first for a hard problem usually gets the work, and level often tracks that trust. Being known as someone who gets things done brings opportunities even without a senior title.

Another panelist says title is one way through the door, not the only way. A person can be trusted with larger scope than their title suggests if a manager or senior sponsor vouches for them, and their own actions build that trust. A director-level sponsor can push for the scope, but the person still has to go find it.

blocks.question: How do you get visibility without feeling that you are self-promoting?
answer: A panelist says visibility is necessary to move up, even when it feels awkward or the person is reserved. Visibility does not mean posting about every win. It can come from giving tech talks after a major launch, running a talk series that brings others in, or answering questions on an internal forum. The key is that the people who speak for you know what you do.

Another panelist adds that an internal brand comes from being approachable and helping teammates get unblocked. A promotion case usually needs peer feedback from three or four co-workers who can vouch for the person. Reaching across disciplines, such as product managers and data scientists, strengthens that case, because a person who wins over only one group is still not moving up.

blocks.question: What was the main reason to seek promotion: money, title, or work-life balance?
answer: One panelist says the main reason was the kind of work. Senior and principal engineers at Amazon were doing influence-heavy work, such as mentoring people, helping engineers grow, and shaping decisions above their own team. The panelist wanted that work. Pay was welcome, but it was not the main draw.

followups.question: Does moving up change pay in a meaningful way?
answer: A panelist says pay at big tech does not rise evenly with level. The jump from senior to staff is usually much larger than the jumps before it, and more of total pay shifts into stock. Money gives optionality, but stock adds risk. Another panelist recalls a grant worth about $1.5 million on paper that was worth roughly $600,000 six months later, after the share price fell. That panelist also says stock outcomes vary across companies and years.

followups.question: Does a well-known employer still help after you leave?
answer: A panelist says pedigree matters because people pattern-match. A name-brand company, such as a staff role at a large tech employer, can set a floor on a later job or a startup. The panelist acknowledges that pattern-matching can also work against people, including on race and gender, and calls that obviously bad. The benefit still mattered to the panelist's own job hopping.

blocks.question: How many people does a staff engineer typically affect?
answer: A panelist thinks about the number of people affected rather than team size. A senior engineer should affect at least their own team and the scope of the senior manager above them. The panel's rough estimates are about 20 to 30 engineers at senior, up to 50 to 60 at staff, and into the hundreds at principal, which can mean a VP's organization.
Another panelist recalls an Airbnb marketplace organization of about 75 engineers, with around five staff engineers within it.

blocks.question: How does office politics affect advancement, and what should people do about it?
answer: A panelist says politics is mostly about people. Some colleagues are difficult, and some use relationships to get ahead in harmful ways. The panelist does not expect a person to change or remove those colleagues, so the better move is to raise your own standing. If the environment is truly toxic, the right answer may be a different place.
The same panelist adds that when people talk about politics, they often mean difficulty communicating with executives or with another team. That gap can be fixed, and fixing it is part of the job.

followups.question: How can someone who is right but blunt get their ideas heard?
answer: A panelist says a manager once told them they were right on most points, but that the way they said things was too blunt for people to hear. The panelist learned to ask questions instead of declaring an idea wrong, to ask whether a design would hold at a larger scale, and to point to an earlier system that had failed in a similar way. The panelist says being heard matters more than being right, and that the questions a person asks can be a sign of intelligence.

Captions carry no speaker labels, so speakers are named only where the transcript identifies them through direct address or first-person detail: Zach (Netflix graph database, Airbnb pricing work, the Airbnb committee comments), Ryan (the ads project and senior promotion; the infrastructure-team remark, inferred from a later cross-reference), Carly (managing staff engineers and year-end review timing), and Lee (promotions trailing). Other turns are attributed to 'a panelist' or 'another panelist'. Captions spell the manager both Carly and Karly; this section uses Carly. Questions are editorial paraphrases of the moderator or chat prompts. Estimates are the panelists' own recollections and are not verified: the share of promotion requests that were premature, team sizes by level, hours worked, pay jumps, the 80 percent pay increase, and the stock figures.
